content: The authors of the report express their deep gratitude to numerous individuals who contributed their expertise, advice, discussions, assistance, and data at various stages of the project. Veronica Luque for discussions about the European Childhood Obesity Project (CHOP) study. Lital Keinan-Boker, Rebecca Goldsmith, Tal Shimony, and Lesley Nitsan for discussions about Israeli data. The report also details the modeling questions addressed by the WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) using the Optifood modeling system. Optifood employs a multi-objective optimization approach called goal programming, which allows for the simultaneous modeling of multiple objectives, such as meeting various nutrient requirements. The system identifies solutions that minimize nutrient gaps while adhering to constraints like energy intake levels and minimum/maximum consumption frequencies for defined food groups and subgroups. The GDG used Optifood to explore several specific questions, including: 1. Whether nutrient needs can be met with unfortified best-case food patterns and what these patterns look like. 2. The impact of eliminating food groups or subgroups. 3. The effects of monotonous staple food consumption. 4. The consequences of modifying the amount of starchy staple foods. 5. The implications of adding unhealthy foods or beverages. 6. The effects of incorporating fortified foods or products. 7. The nutrient gaps observed in real-world food patterns and whether these gaps can be addressed using fortified products. The modeling process began with the development of feasible best-case food patterns, which allowed for generous but realistic quantities of nutrient-dense food subgroups. These patterns served as the starting point for subsequent analyses. The final question regarding real-world food patterns was approached through calculations rather than modeling. The report also outlines the methods used, including the selection of age groups, energy intake levels, and feeding groups for modeling. Energy requirements were estimated based on systematic reviews and were adjusted for different body sizes within each age group. Nutrient reference values (NRVs) were selected from authoritative sources, such as the US and Canadian Dietary Reference Intakes (DRIs) and the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) Dietary Reference Values (DRVs). The GDG prioritized certain nutrients, such as choline and potassium, for inclusion as modeling targets, while others, like protein and niacin, were considered less critical for the specific context of the study. The report emphasizes that while the modeling exercise provides valuable insights, additional work would be required to develop comprehensive food-based recommendations for specific settings.
